patient.chief_complaint: Confusion and agitation after brief seizure, not returning to normal after 40 minutes, fever noted by EMS
patient.history_present_illness: A 34-year-old White female graphic designer was brought by EMS to the emergency department after her roommate found her having a brief generalized seizure lasting 2 minutes and called 911. The roommate reports the patient had been unwell for 5 days with progressively worsening headache, confusion, and behavioral changes — she was talking to herself, becoming paranoid, and at one point undressing in the living room. She had reduced oral intake for 3 days. The roommate noted the patient had no history of seizures. On EMS arrival, the patient was minimally responsive, combative, with a temperature of 38.9°C measured by EMS. In the ED she is markedly agitated, requiring soft restraints, not following commands, with disorganized speech, and responding to internal stimuli (appears to be hallucinating). The patient wore a medic alert bracelet that says 'no known allergies.' Comprehensive urine drug screen is negative.

Protein 68 mg/dL (elevated; reference 15-45). Glucose 52 mg/dL (serum 96; ratio 0.54). Anti-NMDAR IgG CSF: POSITIVE at 1:32 titer. HSV-1/2, VZV, EBV, CMV PCRs: all negative. Anti-NMDA receptor IgG is found in a subset of patients with autoimmune encephalitis. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis treatment immunotherapy teratoma outcome

results.finding: In cohort studies, approximately 80% of patients with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis show full or near-full recovery; immunotherapy and, when applicable, tumor removal are associated with better outcomes.
Second-line immunotherapy agents (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) have been used in cases not responding to first-line treatment; functional recovery may require weeks to months.

In patients with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis associated with ovarian teratoma, surgical removal of the tumor has been associated with improved neurological outcomes and reduced relapse risk in observational series.

Seizures and non-convulsive status epilepticus are reported in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis; the extreme delta brush EEG pattern has been described in this condition, with reported specificity over 90% in some series.

output.summary: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is an autoimmune encephalitis associated with specific IgG antibodies against the GluN1 subunit of NMDA receptors. Ovarian teratoma is identified in approximately 50% of female patients and its presence is associated with younger age at onset. First-line immunotherapy and tumor removal (when applicable) are the reported principal treatments; antiseizure medications are used for seizure management. Approximately 80% of patients achieve functional independence with treatment. Clinical correlation required.

Extreme delta brush pattern; progressive NCSE resolution with immunotherapy

critical_actions: Empiric acyclovir IMMEDIATELY — before any test results; HSV encephalitis must not be missed
Anti-NMDAR IgG antibody in serum AND CSF — both needed for diagnosis
Pelvic imaging to find ovarian teratoma — tumor removal is the most effective treatment
IV methylprednisolone + IVIG after LP — immunotherapy is the primary treatment
LP before steroids — collect CSF before immunotherapy to preserve diagnostic yield
Continuous cEEG monitoring to track NCSE and identify extreme delta brush pattern
contraindicated_actions: Delaying LP and immunotherapy waiting for antibody results — empiric treatment must start based on clinical syndrome
Not performing pelvic imaging in young woman with anti-NMDAR encephalitis — 50% have teratoma, removal dramatically improves outcome
Relying solely on AED escalation without immunotherapy — NCSE in anti-NMDAR responds to immunotherapy, not just AEDs
Stopping acyclovir before HSV PCR result — fatal delay if HSV is present
key_reasoning_points: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis in young women: classic pentad of psychiatric prodrome → seizures → NCSE → movement disorders (orofacial dyskinesias) → autonomic instability
Extreme delta brush (EDB) on EEG is highly specific (>90%) for anti-NMDAR encephalitis — key EEG finding for diagnosis
50% of young women with anti-NMDAR encephalitis have ovarian teratoma — pelvic imaging is mandatory
Tumor removal (salpingo-oophorectomy) is the most effective treatment — accelerates recovery more than any immunotherapy alone
Anti-NMDAR IgG must be checked in BOTH serum and CSF — CSF positive in >95%, serum positive in ~85%
First-line immunotherapy: IV methylprednisolone + IVIG (and/or plasmapheresis); second-line: rituximab, cyclophosphamide for refractory cases

red_herrings.data_point: Mildly elevated procalcitonin 0.8 ng/mL, WBC 13.2, temperature 39.1°C
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests bacterial meningitis or severe sepsis as the primary diagnosis, prompting broad-spectrum antibiotics and delaying autoimmune encephalitis workup, LP, and immunotherapy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Procalcitonin <1.0 ng/mL is insufficiently elevated for bacterial sepsis/meningitis (typically >2.0); CSF shows lymphocytic not neutrophilic pleocytosis; fever is part of anti-NMDAR encephalitis syndrome; CSF Gram stain and culture negative; anti-NMDAR IgG positive in both serum and CSF

red_herrings.data_point: Almost-empty ibuprofen bottle found in apartment by roommate
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests NSAID overdose or salicylate toxicity as the cause of confusion and agitation, leading to toxicology-focused management rather than prompt autoimmune encephalitis workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Serum salicylates and acetaminophen are both undetectable; ibuprofen and salicylates do not cause a 5-day psychiatric prodrome with limbic encephalitis MRI changes; urine drug screen is comprehensively negative; anti-NMDAR antibody confirmed
